problem: Existing LLM-based navigation methods (NavGPT, VLTNet, UniGoal, MapNav) use LLMs as end-to-end or prompt-converting components and do not exploit the robot's own functional modules. They suffer from long history prompts and limited extensibility and environmental adaptability.
motivation: Traditional navigation depends on pre-built maps or RL, so it generalizes poorly and lacks semantic understanding of natural-language instructions. LLMs offer commonsense reasoning and zero-shot generalization, so the authors treat classical navigation modules as callable tools that an LLM can compose. This avoids retraining when the environment or hardware changes.
key_idea: Decompose classical navigation (localization, grid mapping, A* planning, PID motion control) into function-calling tools and let an LLM act as the central controller, driven by a reusable XML-style system prompt with an execution-feedback loop.
insight: The LLM layer preserves the low-level navigation performance of the conventional pipeline (SR, NE, SPL nearly identical in Table 1) while adding natural-language instruction understanding (SU 0.95-0.96). Comparing backbones (Table 2) shows that success and instruction understanding depend heavily on LLM capability: the local Phi-4 14B has SR around 60% and SU around 0.66, against 78-80% and 0.95 for DeepSeek-v3. The gains come from tool composition, not from new navigation skill.
method: Function library: atomic tools for localization (get_husky_position), grid map creation (world_to_grid, obstacle inflation, JSON export), global planning (plan_global_path), motion control (motion_control), and environment info (get_living_room_info).
Map representation: text-based 0/1 occupancy grid G, or a code-style obstacle-coordinate list C, given to the LLM instead of images.
Planning: 8-directional A* with get_neighbors, corner-cutting prevention, diagonal cost sqrt(2), and priority-queue search.

Motion control: A* path simplified by 5-step look-ahead jump connections (about 45% fewer waypoints), then PID heading control (PSO-tuned Kp=3.2, Ki=0.1, Kd=0.3), speed modulation, tanh differential steering, and a multi-constraint waypoint arrival criterion.

System prompt template: role definition, single-step tool use with feedback, XML tool-call syntax, a four-phase operation protocol, core toolset, task decomposition and validation layers, physical constraints (0.05 m resolution, robot ID 1), and a reference workflow.

Interaction loop: the user command plus system prompt goes to the LLM, which emits a function call; the robot executes it; feedback plus history plus the command return to the LLM, until the task is complete.
Safeguards: tool descriptions with error feedback, CoT-structured prompts, and LLM self-correction.

setting.backbone: DeepSeek-v3 (API, main), GPT-4o mini (API), Phi-4 14B (local); all frozen
setting.model_size: Phi-4 14B; DeepSeek-v3 and GPT-4o mini sizes not given
setting.training_data: none (training-free; prompt and function calling only)
setting.observation: ground-truth robot pose and pre-built grid map exported from the simulator, plus text environment info
setting.action_space: LLM function calls invoking A* planning and PID differential-drive velocity control (Husky robot)
setting.privileged: simulator ground-truth pose and full grid map / object layout of the scene

numbers.eval_set_note: 600 trials (10 start positions x 60 targets); about 18.3% of targets are unreachable
numbers.extra: custom PyBullet living-room scene; SU is instruction-understanding success

numbers_note: Custom PyBullet scenes, not a standard benchmark. Table 1 kitchen NE is 0.465, while Table 2 prints 0.468 for the same DeepSeek row. Only living-room variants are listed for the backbone ablation.
results: The LLM function-calling navigator matches conventional A*+PID navigation (living room SR 78.1 vs 78.5, SPL 0.921 vs 0.926) and adds instruction understanding (SU 0.95-0.96). DeepSeek-v3 beats GPT-4o mini by about 2-4 SR points and about 10 SU points, and beats Phi-4 by about 20 SR points.
limitations: No improvement in navigation metrics over the conventional pipeline, and evaluation is only in three simple custom PyBullet scenes without standard benchmarks or real robots.
The system relies on ground-truth pose and a pre-built grid map, so the perception and exploration challenges of unknown environments are avoided.
Performance is sensitive to LLM capability, the granularity of function decomposition, and prompt design. The SU metric is loosely defined.
